subject: english-language

moments.title: Piaget's stages
moments.body: 1920s-60s: Piaget develops a stage theory of cognitive development — sensorimotor (0-2), preoperational (2-7), concrete operational (7-11), formal operational (11+). Language acquisition is tied to cognitive development; egocentric speech becomes inner thought.
moments.takeaway: Piaget's stages are influential but later research has shown more continuous development than his stage theory predicted. Children often show abilities earlier than Piaget thought.

moments.title: Vygotsky's social development
moments.body: 1920s-30s: Vygotsky develops his own theory — language is fundamentally social, learned in interaction with more capable peers and adults. The 'Zone of Proximal Development' is the gap between what a child can do alone and with help. 'Scaffolding' (Jerome Bruner's later term, 1976) is the support that enables learning.
moments.takeaway: Vygotsky died young (1934) and his work was suppressed in the Soviet Union for decades. He became widely known in the West only after 1960s translations.

moments.title: Modern synthesis
moments.body: Bruner, Wood and Ross (1976) introduce 'scaffolding' as the support that helps a learner achieve more than they could alone — building on Vygotsky. Modern education theory often blends Piagetian and Vygotskyan ideas. Cognitive load theory, sociocultural theory all extend the framework.
moments.takeaway: Modern child language acquisition research (Tomasello, Lieven) draws on both Piaget and Vygotsky alongside contemporary cognitive science.

now.title: Educational application
now.body: Piaget and Vygotsky remain on A-level Language and Psychology syllabuses. Scaffolding is mainstream educational practice. Modern child development research has substantially complicated both stage and social-only accounts. The combined Piaget-Vygotsky synthesis shapes much teacher training.
now.open_questions: How important is interaction vs maturation? The modern answer is both. The relative weighting varies by context, child and theorist.

reflection: Two early-20th-century theorists — one Swiss, one Soviet — defined competing accounts of how children develop. Modern child development theory blends and refines them. Their key insights — Piaget's structured development, Vygotsky's social learning — are now mainstream.
